solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One's helpless when upset, in cruel truth

indicators.note: when upset says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A sympathetic remark that someone is powerless when distressed, delivered as a harsh but honest observation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when upset' turns the letters ELTRUT, which straddle 'cruel truth', backwards. The definition hints at a creature flipped onto its back, unable to right itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelled reptile turned over on its back cannot right itself, so it is the creature that is helpless when upset.

clue.text: Sweetheart once seen in Pudding Lane?

definitions.meaning: a former lover or past romantic partner
the Great Fire of London began in a bakery in Pudding Lane in 1666, so an ancient blaze was seen there

explanation.surface: Someone spots a former lover while strolling down a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Pudding Lane in the City of London is where the Great Fire of 1666 started, so the second reading is a literal fire from long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: A past romantic partner is idiomatically called this; the second sense is a historic fire, the blaze of 1666.

clue.text: Below par — where we all are most of the time!

definitions.meaning: feeling unwell, not up to usual form

definitions.text: where we all are most of the time!
definitions.meaning: taken literally, people live beneath the sky's conditions of rain, cloud and sun

explanation.surface: A wry grumble that everyone feels rather off-colour nearly all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition takes the idiom literally: we all live beneath the clouds and rain.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means slightly ill or off-colour, which is what feeling below par describes.

clue.text: With more leaves, replanted beer garden's not bad

indicators.note: replanted suggests the letters are set out again in a new arrangement
not says the letters of the following word are left out of the mix

parts.note: the possessive 's adds no letter, leaving the two words as written
these three letters are the ones taken away from the pool

explanation.surface: A pub's garden has been replanted and now looks rather pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replanted' rearranges the letters of BEER GARDEN, and 'not bad' says the letters B, A and D are left out of the mix: a subtractive (composite) anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of the colour of foliage describes something leafier, with more verdant growth.

clue.text: Where one turns for treatment and neat sheets?

definitions.meaning: taken literally, the bends in the corridors of a medical institution
tightly folded bedding at the ends of a made bed

explanation.surface: A patient heads off for medical care while someone admires a tidily made bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is literal: the bends you go round inside an infirmary on the way to be treated.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurses fold bedlinen with tight diagonal tucks at the mattress ends, giving the neat sheets the clue mentions.

clue.text: Put shirt on but lost it, apparently?

definitions.meaning: to stake everything one has, as in a bet
someone who has lost the shirt is left wearing only an undershirt

explanation.surface: Someone bets heavily on something and then seems to have lost the lot.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'put one's shirt on' something is a British idiom for betting everything; the second reading splits the answer as IN VEST, the undergarment left after losing a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Committing money to a venture in hope of return is what putting your shirt on something does.

clue.text: Execrate tailless dogs

indicators.note: tailless says the final letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: to execrate is to curse or damn

explanation.surface: Someone swears at a pack of dogs whose tails have been docked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' looks like it describes the dogs, but it docks the last letter E from CURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mongrels or worthless dogs are an old synonym, used as a plural noun here.

clue.text: Struggle with Derek about university entrance …

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round the other

parts.note: Del is a short form of the name Derek, as in Del Boy

indicators.note: the entrance of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone has a tussle with a man called Derek over getting into university.
explanation.walkthrough: DEL, a familiar form of Derek, goes 'about' U, the opening letter of 'university'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fight between two parties, or any close contest, is a struggle.

clue.text: … and not Norman

definitions.meaning: the conjunction used after a negative, meaning also not
the standard abbreviation of Norman is these three letters

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: and not some fellow named Norman.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to the one before, but the clue stands alone: a conjunction plus an abbreviation of Norman.
explanation.definitionFit: The conjunction that continues a negative statement means 'and not', as in neither this nor that.

clue.text: Comes clean during home-grown supper …

indicators.note: during says the answer sits within the following words

explanation.surface: Someone confesses the truth over a meal made from home-grown produce.
explanation.definitionFit: To confess or admit a wrong is the phrasal-verb idiom meaning to come clean.

clue.text: … itself chaotically put an end to

indicators.note: chaotically says the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Something descends into chaos and so brings about its own end.
explanation.definitionFit: To suppress or smother something, as in stifling a revolt, is to put an end to it.

clue.text: Stimulating stuff from former reporters and leader in Observer

parts.note: ex- means former, as in ex-wife
the press is the body of journalists or reporters

indicators.note: the leader in a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Ex-journalists and an Observer editorial supply a stimulant, as if newsroom coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' looks like a newspaper editorial, which fits The Observer, a British Sunday paper, but it just means the first letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong black coffee is a stimulant; this variant spelling of the Italian coffee name is accepted in British dictionaries.

clue.text: Disorderly temp arrested — not in Harrods, maybe

indicators.note: disorderly means jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An unruly temporary worker is arrested, but not inside the famous London shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disorderly' seems to describe the temp, but it shuffles TEMP ARRESTED NOT. Harrods is a famous luxury shop in Knightsbridge, London.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrods is an example of a large retail emporium selling many kinds of goods in separate sections.

clue.text: Eggs are rank, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says a word is identified by how it is pronounced

parts.note: a rank is a row or line, as of soldiers

explanation.surface: A complaint that some eggs smell foul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rank' looks like an adjective for smelly eggs, but it is a noun meaning a line, ROW, said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Fish eggs, in a mass, are a culinary term for spawn, as in cod's roe.

clue.text: Licensee debarring Radiohead musician

indicators.note: debarring means shutting out, so one letter is removed

parts.note: a taverner is the keeper of a tavern, the holder of a drinks licence
the head of the word radio is its first letter R

explanation.surface: A pub landlord bans a member of the rock band Radiohead.
explanation.walkthrough: Radiohead is a British rock band, but here it means the head of 'radio', R. Sir John Tavener was an English composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Tavener was an English composer of sacred music, so he is an example of a musician.

clue.text: Proxima Centauri — central star

indicators.note: central says the letters are taken from the very middle of the phrase

explanation.surface: An astronomy note: the nearest star to the Sun is the main one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star' seems astronomical but means an expert; the middle three of the fifteen letters of 'Proxima Centauri' supply it.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert or outstanding performer, such as a flying hero, is figuratively a star.

clue.text: Round the borders of Tiree, tartan's woven

indicators.note: round means one piece goes around the other

parts.note: a plaid is a tartan cloth

indicators.note: the borders of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: On the Scottish island of Tiree, tartan cloth is woven all around.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiree is a small island in the Scottish Inner Hebrides; its 'borders' are T and E, inside PLAID.
explanation.definitionFit: Strands interlaced like a braid are woven together, as hair or rope can be.

clue.text: "Protect from sun"? Me, I'm off on to island

indicators.note: on to says the jumbled letters are placed after the next piece
off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, the apostrophe giving no letter

explanation.surface: Someone shielding from the sun on a beach says they are heading out to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' shuffles SUN ME I'M into MMUNISE, which goes 'on to' I for island.
explanation.definitionFit: To make resistant to disease, especially by vaccination, is to protect someone.

clue.text: Battens down (28s, etc?) with this agreement

indicators.note: down suggests the letters are knocked over into a new order

explanation.surface: A treaty that shuts down missile silos, with the cross-reference pointing to another answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference to 28 points to missile silos, which a nuclear treaty would close down. 'down' rearranges BATTENS.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty banning nuclear weapons trials is an international agreement.

clue.text: Svelte fop led men designing personal enhancement

indicators.note: designing means making something new, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A slim dandy guides male designers toward improving themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Improving one's own abilities and character is personal enhancement.

clue.text: Betrothed, half-cut, is in France entering carnival

indicators.note: entering means one piece goes inside the other
half-cut says the word loses half of its letters

parts.note: a fiancé is a man who is betrothed
est is French for is

explanation.surface: A tipsy engaged couple join in a French carnival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-cut' is British slang for drunk, but here it chops FIANCE to FIA; EST, French for 'is', goes 'entering' that.
explanation.definitionFit: A festival or public celebration with merrymaking, as in Spain, is a carnival.

clue.text: Head swaps a penny for nothing — simpleton!

indicators.note: swaps says one letter is exchanged for another

parts.note: noddle is an informal word for the head
d is the abbreviation for an old British penny
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An insult: someone's head is so empty they'd trade a coin for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the old British penny (from Latin denarius); NODDLE swaps one D for O.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal word for a foolish person or simpleton, also slang for the head.

clue.text: See you at about ten, prepared to go into "Life Story"

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round the other

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to go into says one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: a bio is a short life story, a biography

indicators.note: prepared means made ready, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An arrangement to meet at about ten o'clock, ready for a biography.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' rearranges TEN to ENT, which goes into BIO, and AT goes 'about' the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: This French phrase is a farewell meaning until soon, the same as 'see you' in English.

clue.text: Pitt's fixer?

definitions.meaning: the first name of the American actor Pitt
a small thin nail, which fixes things together

explanation.surface: Who solves the Hollywood star's problems?
explanation.walkthrough: 'fixer' suggests an agent who sorts out trouble; it is a type of nail.
explanation.definitionFit: A small flat-headed nail fixes things in place; it is also the actor Pitt's first name.

clue.text: Sergeant regularly enjoins cook to get married

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: A sergeant routinely orders the cook to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the even letters of ENJOINS COOK, giving NONCO.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a non-commissioned officer, abbreviated as this hyphenated term.

clue.text: Tennis-player Andrew showing how to move on baseline

definitions.meaning: Andrew ... is a British former tennis player and broadcaster
a chess move along the back rank where king and rook both shift

explanation.surface: A tennis player shows how to move along the baseline of a court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baseline' suggests a tennis court, but it is the back row of a chessboard, where the king and rook make a special move together. Andrew Castle is a British former tennis player turned TV presenter.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess, the king and a rook move together on the back rank in one special manoeuvre.

clue.text: Bearing with voluble beneficiary

indicators.note: voluble means talkative, so the word is identified by being spoken

parts.note: an heir benefits from a will

explanation.surface: A chatty person who inherits carries themselves with poise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'voluble' signals that HEIR, a will's beneficiary, is spoken; its silent H makes it sound right.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's manner or demeanour, as in an air of confidence, is their bearing.

clue.text: Lois's dressing chamber

indicators.note: dressing suggests the letters are rearranged, as a wound is dressed

parts.note: the possessive 's adds no letter, so the name is taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman named Lois has her own dressing room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressing chamber' reads as a dressing room; 'dressing' rearranges LOIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A tower or pit used to store grain, or an underground missile chamber.
